text.content: Acyberpunk genre character largely uses the same rules as other Modern AGE characters, but with new options, and a few new special systems to accommodate cyberpunk’s classic technologies and motifs. Naturally if you’re a player, you should check with the Game Master about what kind of characters the campaign can accommodate and check with your fellow players so your character’s abilities complement those of the other protagonists.

The following sections will take you through the character creation process in Modern AGE as it applies to cyberpunk genre characters in this book.

Step 1: Concept

The cyberpunk genre can fit most character concepts that don’t rely on the supernatural, but classic works tend to favor the concepts also found in film noir, hardboiled fiction, pulp, and technothriller genres. These generally feature highly competent characters whose cynicism may or may not conceal a strong moral center. That’s not all cyberpunk is, however; technology raises questions about everything from political freedoms to personal identity. What kind of people arise in a world where you can customize your body at will, but this, alongside the necessities of life, prompts a ruthless struggle for survival in a worn-out society? The unifying feature of the genre is ultimately esthetic, because cyberpunk has been around for over 40 years: long enough to have spawned innumerable approaches and variations using a common set of ideas.

Biological Versus Synthetic

The cyberpunk genre introduces the possibility of characters who are transferred to, or artificial consciousnesses inhabiting, an constructed body, such as a cyborg or robot. At this stage, the origin of the character’s mind requires no special rules considerations, but unlike most Modern AGE games, Step 1 has a firm rules element: You must choose a biological or synthetic body. Since one emphasis of these rules is on ease of use, don’t overthink the “realistic” implications of one type compared to the other. In the absence of specific rules or Game Master guidance to the contrary, assume things work as per default Modern AGE.

Biological Bodies

The Modern AGE rules assume biological bodies are the norm, so no special rules apply beyond any other rules that refer to them here. However, note that artificially produced bodies that strongly resemble living organisms (such as androids that need to breathe, and eat, and which get wounded and heal like natural organisms) should be biological, not synthetic.

Synthetic bodies begin with two of the following vulnerabilities, or similar vulnerabilities designed by the GM.

Corrupt Senses: The interface between your brain and your body’s sensory feeds is flawed. When you roll a 1 on the Stunt Die for any test that relies on your senses, the GM may feed you false information. This fake data has an ultimate source, whether it is from your psyche filling in missing pieces, errant pattern recognition systems, or an antagonistic AI in the server that updates your mind. You may not be initially aware of the problem, but it can be found by a character with the Intelligence (Synthlife) focus (TN 13).

Fueled: You require an external power source other than simple electricity and the various components The GM should assume you scrounge to maintain yourself between adventures. These could be specialized batteries you must replace periodically, or even food, for quasi-biological systems.

Hackable: Your body has the connectivity and security flaws required for unwanted remote access. See Chapter 4 for information on hacking synthetic bodies and minds. If anyone’s body can be hacked, no matter its origin, do not use this vulnerability, since all characters have it anyway.

Obvious: You are obviously artificial. It takes little more than a glance or touch to confirm you have a synthetic body, and hiding it is difficult—you take a -3 penalty to Communication

(Disguise) tests intended to conceal your nature.

Recharges: You should spend at least ¼ of your time in standby mode, recharging in a state of total inactivity except for your thoughts and senses. After 18 hours of continuous operation, you suffer a cumulative -1 penalty all somatic and mixed ability tests, and a cumulative -2 penalty to Speed, for each additional hour of activity, until at the 24th hour and beyond, when you cannot act, move, or sense your surroundings. Every hour of this penalized overtime requires an hour of compensatory rest, which removes penalties in the reverse of the order they were applied, but unless you rest for 6 hours on top of that, the penalties will immediately accumulate again. Outside such a low power emergency, however, you can split up your recharges, if they take a minimum of 1 hour each, and occupy a total of 6 hours out of every 24. You can have both the recharge and fueled vulnerabilities, indicating you require an unusual fuel source as well as rest. Taken together, they can represent the need to eat and sleep.

Temperamental: Unless carefully maintained, your body tends to break down in unexpected ways. When you roll a 1 on a failed test using a somatic or mixed ability during a game session, you become aware something is about to act up, but you’re not necessarily sure what. On your next failed somatic or mixed ability test, consult the Stunt Die. You gain a Complication (see Sample Complications in Chapter 3, equal in point value to the result. Fortunately, a character with the proper equipment can make a TN 13 Intelligence (Synthlife) and one hour to reduce the Complication’s strength by the test’s degree of success. A technician can perform this maintenance pre-emptively as well. Fortunately, you can’t gain more than two Complications at a time—hold off checking whether others might arise until at least one existing Complication is gone.

Unshielded: Your body is exceptionally reactive to electromagnetic fields. All damaging electrical hazards inflicts an additional 1d6 damage on you. Strong electromagnetic fields others may find harmless may injure or influence you, at the GM’s discretion.

Synthetic Bodies

Synthetic bodes, such as those possessed by robots or cyborgs whose bodies are almost entirely artificial, have basic capabilities roughly equivalent to those of human bodies—no superior strength, speed, or intellect. They have the following characteristics:

  • Abiotic Resilience: Synthetic bodies are immune to hazards that inflict damage by interfering with functions like respiration, digestion, and other biological characteristics. The Game Master determines the extent of this immunity, but it usually means characters in synthetic bodies cannot be poisoned or suffocated, at least. Default synthetic bodies have the same tolerances as human bodies when it comes to temperature extremes. The precise type of body can fine tune these capabilities—a cyborg might still need to breathe, for instance.
  • Abiotic Vulnerability: Synthetic bodies may have inherent disadvantages, design flaws, and other factors that make them vulnerable to hazards their

biological counterparts are either immune to, or are not as adversely affected by. Choose two options from the Abiotic Vulnerabilities sidebar, or alternatives you and the GM agree upon. In some campaigns, however, all synthetic characters may have one or more vulnerabilities in common.

  • Capacity Bonus: Synthetic bodies’ constructed nature makes them easier to modify, granting +1 Capacity slot for augmentations above the default number in the campaign. See Chapter 3: Cyberpunk Augmentations for more information. If you switch to a biological body, you lose this bonus slot.
  • Damaged, Not Injured: Synthetic bodies cannot benefit from the First Aid action, and do not heal through breathers or rest. When reduced to 0 Health, they cease to function immediately, but don’t die—they just become non-functional until repaired, though characters with biological components will perish in 5 + Constitution hours. Characters with synthetic bodies can be killed with a coup de grace (Modern AGE Basic Rulebook, p. 40), but unlike biological bodies, the attack

This supplement is deliberately vague about the boundaries of biological versus synthetic life. In some games, synthetics are robots made of metal, advanced composites, and electronics. Other settings may use nanotechnology to simulate life or place a thin but firm divide between natural-bodied characters and artificially created individuals who might be called androids, bioroids, replicants, and so forth.

In practical terms, this rough split lets us design rules covering the widest possible range of campaigns. You could, for example, create a party of renegade synthetic characters who appear human, but who are slated for “retirement” for outliving their original functions. This approach also allows you to add a robot character to a party of humans or portray a consciousness that shifts between natural and artificial bodies.

If the Game Master has firm ideas about the technologies in play, they may further divide or restrict the applicability of the Intelligence (Synthlife) focus or Synthtech talent. In some campaigns, nanotech constructions, genetically engineered life, and robotics are all separate disciplines. In others, all synthetic characters are genetically engineered. Remember, however, that artificial characters with human physical vulnerabilities are considered biological. The GM should work out any ambiguities when designing the campaign and guide players through making their characters.

  • Repairable: Although synthetic bodies do not heal on their own, they can benefit from a variation of extended medical attention (Modern AGE Basic Rulebook, p. 46). This functions the same as for biological bodies, except sleep provides no benefit to stack with, and the test is made with Intelligence (Synthlife—see Cyberpunk Focuses later in this chapter) instead of Intelligence (Medicine). Talents that improve healing for biological bodies do not do so for synthetic bodies, but this chapter features alternatives in the Cyberpunk Talents section of this chapter.

Step 2: Abilities

Generate abilities using the whatever standard Modern AGE rules the Game Master and your play group favors.

Noetic, Somatic, and Mixed Abilities

In some cyberpunk campaigns characters can transfer their minds to new bodies. This can take the form of messy, complex surgery that implants the character’s brain and central nervous system in a new body; destructive uploading, which records mental data digitally with a method that destroys the source brain; and non-destructive uploading or copying, which brings about the possibility of a single consciousness “forking” into multiple bodies, with each iteration changing as their embodied experiences do. Furthermore, some circumstances, such as entering virtual worlds, may “transport” the character’s mind, but not their body.

These possibilities necessitate splitting abilities into three categories: somatic, noetic, and mixed.

Noetic Abilities

Noetic abilities transfer into any body as part of the character’s mind. The destination body virtually never influences these abilities, so unless the GM devises unusual circumstances, they hop from body to body, unaltered. The noetic abilities are Communication, Intelligence, and Willpower.

Somatic Abilities

Somatic abilities are a function of the character’s current body. When a character’s mind enters a new body, they take on the somatic abilities of that body. The somatic abilities are Constitution, Dexterity, and Strength.

Mixed Abilities and Capacity

Mixed abilities rely on both mind and body. For game purposes, the character’s mind possesses these abilities, while their destination bodies modify them. A body with standard human capabilities applies a modifier of 0 to mixed abilities. Adjustments change if the character inhabits a new body.

The mixed abilities are Accuracy, Fighting, and Perception. Furthermore, your Capacity to integrate augmentation, as measured in slots and fully described in Chapter 3, is handled like a mixed ability, as the base slots “belong” to your mind, but can be influenced by the body you’re in.

Ability Focuses

Cyberpunk genre games feature new focuses. These are discussed in the Cyberpunk Character Options section, later in this chapter.

Step 3: Background

All backgrounds listed in the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook could exist in a typical cyberpunk setting. However, the following are especially suited to the genre: Academic, Corporate, Military, and Outcast. These are incorporated into the alternative background tables which the GM can use instead of the standard Modern AGE tables. As usual, the GM and play group can always pick backgrounds instead of rolling for them randomly. The Modern AGE Companion also tells you how to create backgrounds from scratch.

In addition, some characters have the option of swapping out background benefits for special qualities. These are traits provided by the futuristic technological milieu. They include additional augmentation Capacity slots. See Chapter 3: Cyber-

In most cases, only artificially-modified bodies confer mixed ability modifiers. However, some characters may have genetic or epigenetic exceptionalities, or synthetic counterparts to these, which might affect new inhabitants. If the Game Master chooses a body whose previous inhabitant had a mixed ability of 5 or 6 confers a +1 bonus, while a rating of 7 (representing the peak of unenhanced human ability) confers a +2 bonus. A mixed ability rating of -3 imposes a -1 penalty. In settings where enhanced Accuracy, Fighting, or Perception are hard to come by, this motivates certain parties to clone or steal the bodies of exceptionally talented characters.

Cyberpunk Backgrounds

The following new backgrounds are appropriate for many cyberpunk genre campaigns.

Capacity slot

You receive one additional augmentation Capacity slot over and above those normally granted to characters in the campaign. You and the GM should discuss whether it is already devoted to augmentations or represents your compatibility with them.

Focus Swap Focus Only

You can swap out a background or profession-granted focus, but not another improvement, for a new focus from this book based on the same ability. This helps update certain backgrounds and professions, but it can also be used to customize the ones detailed here if the GM allows it. For example, you could swap out Accuracy (Longarms) for Accuracy (Drone Weaponry).

Information Processor Background Only

You sort information and crunch numbers with the speed and accuracy of a computer—indeed, this quality is designed for characters with partially or wholly artificial minds, who may never have been human. Therefore, it can only be swapped for a background-based improvement, since it is assumed to be an inherent ability, or one which required a high degree of acclimatization.

You can always choose to succeed at any Intelligence (Cryptography), Intelligence (Mathematics), and Intelligence (Research—digital sources only) test, with a TN of 10 + your Intelligence + focus bonus, though if you choose this option instead of rolling, you gain no stunt points for scoring doubles. You also accomplish these tasks an order of magnitude faster—days become hours, hours become minutes, minutes become rounds, rounds become major actions, major actions become minor actions, and minor actions become a bonus test you may make each round without using an action.

Talent Swap Talent Only

You can swap one talent degree granted by a background or profession for a degree in one of the new talents in this book, if the GM agrees it fits the background or profession’s feel, at least in terms of how the character approaches it, and works in the campaign. Like focus swap this is intended to “upgrade” previous Modern AGE professions to the cyberpunk genre, but it might also be used to modify some of the new backgrounds and professions in this book.

In games where psionic, magical, or other extraordinary powers beyond artificial augmentations are permitted, the character may substitute a talent degree granted by background and profession. for a degree in the applicable talent, or equivalent, permitted by the GM and found in Chapter 6 of the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook or other sources present in the campaign.

Step 4: Profession

Most Modern AGE core professions work well in the cyberpunk genre. In classic examples, the least common are probably Athlete and Clergy (Lower); Politician and Merchant (Upper); and Explorer and Dilettante (Upper). All Outsider professions are appropriate, reflecting the genre’s common focus on outcasts and outlaws. The following section introduces six new professions to replace these less common ones. The GM can of course introduce new professions as well by taking them from Modern AGE books or designing them based on guidance in the Modern AGE Companion.

Like background improvements, those granted by professions can be swapped for the special qualities listed in the SPECIAL QUALITIES FOR BACKGROUNDS AND PROFESSIONS sidebar in this chapter.

The revised profession tables swap the lesser-used ones from the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook for fitting replacements, found here. The Outsider table on p. 18 of the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook is not included, as it remains unchanged.

Step 5: Drive

In cyberpunk genre games, drive employs the standard Modern AGE rules. The Modern AGE Basic Rulebook and Modern AGE Companion both discuss ways to build custom drives. The six options in the Cyberpunk Drives table are included for inspiration, but they’re not the only ones available in a cyberpunk-style campaign.

Steps 6, 7, 8, and 9

These steps all use the standard Modern AGE rules, though a cyberpunk campaign may feature additional options. The new equipment detailed in Chapter 2 is available, and augmentations from Chapter 3 might change derived statistics. Goals, Ties, and Relationships will naturally be influenced by a futuristic campaign world, as will your character’s description.

There’s no reason to ban any focus, talent, or specialization, but depending on the campaign, the Game Master may disallow some of them, or make them difficult to acquire. A dystopian tyranny may make it hard to learn certain artistic or even scientific focuses, for instance. Some campaigns may feature technologies that make certain areas of expertise obsolete as well, though just as in the real, modern world, there are often communities practicing these “dead” skills.

Therefore, the following sections only feature new focuses, talents, and specializations, which the GM and permit or disallow as they please.

Cyberpunk Talents

New tech demands new forms of expertise. The following talents exist for just such reasons in cyberpunk-genre games.

Sacrifice Augmentation Special

If you must, you can sacrifice part of yourself to save the rest. If you are struck by an attack that doesn’t affect an area or inherently target your entire body, you can reduce its damage by [Gritty 5/Pulpy 10/Cinematic 20] per Capacity slot’s worth of augmentations you allow to be critically damaged instead. Partially “used up” augmentations (such as by using a 2 Capacity augmentation to eliminate 4 points of damage) also become non-functional. You used these to shield yourself from the attack at the last moment. You must explain how you accomplished this within the story. Sacrificing a cybernetic arm is easy to describe but absorbing damage with your commlink is probably impossible.

fully defend against an attack or reduce its damage to 0, you gain 1 SP that can be used to take the Adrenaline Rush, Duck and Weave, or Skirmish stunts, or improve the potency of one of the stunts if you took in through another source of SP.

Master: You gain one additional cybercombat quality (three total). Furthermore, you can delay the effects of up to 2 ranks of exceeding your Capacity during action encounters. You do not suffer ability reduction, ignore damage taken as a penalty for exceeding Capacity, and do not suffer complications during these events—but the full effects return after an action scene, and assert themselves on top of any injuries or other disadvantages. Thus, if the Breakdown effect caused you 5 points of damage, you would ignore that damage for the encounter, but if you were reduced to 3 Health at its conclusion, not counting breakdown damage, the end of the encounter would immediately drop you to 0 Health.
